introduction-from-cli-to-control-plane.core: Terraform reconciles only when someone runs apply; between runs, drift goes unnoticed. Crossplane turns Kubernetes into a universal control plane: cloud resources become custom resources, and controllers continuously reconcile them against the cloud, just as the Deployment controller keeps pods running. You get kubectl, RBAC, GitOps and continuous drift correction for databases and buckets.

first_principles.problem: A manually deleted RDS instance stays missing until someone next runs terraform apply, days later.
truths: Kubernetes is a generic control-loop platform.
Same API for apps and infra simplifies tooling.

analogy.title: A thermostat vs flipping the heater manually
analogy.story: You set the temperature once and the thermostat keeps correcting; you don't have to remember to check.
analogy.breaks: Thermostats tolerate a few degrees; controllers correct every drift they see.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Delete it in the console and the controller recreates it within minutes.

kind: Bucket
metadata:
  name: acme-logs
spec:
  forProvider:
    region: us-east-1
  providerConfigRef:

check.q: What's the key operational difference between Crossplane and Terraform?
check.a: Crossplane continuously reconciles via controllers; Terraform only reconciles when someone runs plan/apply.

providers-connecting-crossplane-to-the-c.core: A Crossplane provider is a package that installs CRDs (managed resources such as Bucket or RDSInstance) and a controller that calls the cloud API. ProviderConfig objects supply credentials, ideally via IRSA or workload identity rather than static keys. Upbound's official providers are largely generated from Terraform providers, so coverage is broad; family providers split large clouds into smaller installs.

first_principles.problem: Installing the monolithic AWS provider adds 900 CRDs and slows the API server.
truths: Each provider brings CRDs and a controller.
Too many CRDs burden the API server.

analogy.title: Installing language packs on a phone
analogy.story: Only add the languages you speak; each pack takes space and needs the right keyboard (credentials).
analogy.breaks: Language packs don't create real resources; providers do, with real bills.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Only S3 CRDs installed, keyless auth.

check.a: Deleting the Kubernetes object leaves the cloud resource in place instead of deleting it.

compositions-building-your-own-api.core: Compositions let a platform team define their own abstractions. A CompositeResourceDefinition (XRD) declares a new API (for example `PostgresInstance` with size and version), and a Composition maps it to managed resources (RDS, subnet group, security group, secret), today usually via function pipelines (patch-and-transform, KCL, Go). Developers create a simple claim in their namespace and get a full, compliant database.

first_principles.problem: Developers must understand 40 RDS parameters to get a database, and each team configures it differently.
derivation: Define an **XRD** with a minimal schema.
Write a **Composition** mapping to managed resources.
Write **connection secrets** to the claim's namespace.

analogy.title: A restaurant menu vs the kitchen
analogy.story: Diners order 'medium steak'; the kitchen handles suppliers, temperatures and plating.
analogy.breaks: Menus rarely change; XRD schema changes need versioning.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Encrypted, backed-up, networked RDS from 8 lines.

code.text:
apiVersion: platform.acme.io/v1alpha1
kind: PostgresInstance
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: team-orders
spec:
  size: medium        # composition maps to db.r6g.large, multi-AZ, encrypted
  version: "16"
  writeConnectionSecretToRef: { name: orders-db-conn }

check.q: What is the role of an XRD versus a Composition?
check.a: The XRD defines the schema of the new API; the Composition defines which managed resources implement it.

crossplane-vs-terraform-choosing-the-rig.core: Terraform is mature, has huge provider coverage, explicit plans for review and works without Kubernetes, but reconciles only on apply. Crossplane gives continuous reconciliation, a Kubernetes-native self-service API and GitOps integration, but needs a well-run management cluster, lacks a true plan preview, and debugging spans controllers and events. Many organisations use Terraform for foundations and Crossplane for app-level self-service.

first_principles.problem: A team migrates everything to Crossplane and loses the reviewable plan output that auditors relied on.
truths: Each tool has a different reconciliation model.

analogy.title: A surveyor's plan vs a groundskeeper
analogy.story: The surveyor draws precise plans for big changes; the groundskeeper keeps everything tidy every day.
analogy.breaks: Groundskeepers ask before big changes; controllers just reconcile.

check.q: What capability do teams most often miss when moving from Terraform to Crossplane?
check.a: A reliable plan/preview of exactly what will change before it happens.
